claims.text: A machine-learning framework incorporating defect, impurity, and temperature-dependent scattering will predict bulk HfNbTaTiZr conductivity significantly more accurately than conventional perfect-crystal analytical models.
Experimental bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimens include both defect-minimized material and material containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed model will be trained using both high-fidelity simulations and experimental conductivity data.
The high-fidelity simulations used for training will account for defect and impurity scattering.
The model will use separate parameterizations for 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Electronic scattering in HfNbTaTiZr depends on temperature and is modulated by defect density and oxygen impurities.
Oxygen-induced defects interact nonlinearly with intrinsic temperature-dependent scattering rates.
Representing these interactions allows the model to adjust electron mean free paths and scattering events for realistic microstructures.
Accounting for realistic defect and impurity scattering will improve conductivity predictions relative to traditional analytical models.
The model's predictions will closely match conductivity measurements throughout 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
At approximately 500 K, the predicted conductivity is 1.0×10^6 S/m within ±10%.
Existing analytical predictions assume perfect, defect-free crystals and omit oxygen impurities and realistic defect scattering.
The proposed model is applicable within 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The proposed model is applicable to HfNbTaTiZr containing up to approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Predictions outside the stated temperature ranges or at other impurity concentrations may require additional calibration.
Available high-fidelity defect-scattering simulations may be limited.
Experimental noise is expected to contribute uncertainty, especially in the 0–200 K regime.
A deviation greater than ±10% from 1.0×10^6 S/m at 500 K for the oxygen-containing sample will falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to improve on traditional analytical predictions across the designated temperature ranges will falsify the hypothesis.
